Well, badruns, had a good answer in that software is technically never done, but a mix of things happens.

  • Different features that couldn't be fit into version 1.0 are worked on.
  • Bug fixes (any software more complex than "Hello World" has plenty of bugs that emerge as users hammer away on it)
  • Technical support: users that can't figure out shit need hand holding and assistance. Sometimes they'll report things as bugs that aren't bugs, so you have to waste time trying to decipher their vague descriptions of what's wrong to see if there's even an issue in the first place.
  • Performance optimizations. Something might technically work, but be slow and inefficient. You can go through a program and find slow parts and improve that.
  • Technical debt is resolved. When management decides that a product must be released in 6 months and it takes you 15 months to build it the right way, you might hack together a fucked up solution to get it done in time, but then go back and build something properly that's more flexible and efficient for the future
  • User interface changes are implemented. Once designers and stakeholders see things in action they will change some things.
  • Some team members will move on after a project is released. Maybe if 300 developers are on some project for a few years, after it's released, some of them will quit to maybe take a break and use their accomplishment to find a better job. Some will move on to different projects within a company. So maybe after version 1.0 comes out, there's only a third of the original developers still working on that original project
